title: SEO, accessibility, and performance
summary: Build pages that are discoverable, usable by everyone, and fast on real devices, then verify them with a reproducible audit.

lessons.title: Technical SEO and metadata
prerequisites: Understand semantic HTML, Next.js metadata, and the difference between laboratory and real-user measurement.
Be able to restate “canonical URL” before coding: The preferred address declared to search engines when several URLs may show the same content.
Know how to create exercises/20-web-quality/product-metadata.ts, run npm run build, and compare real output with a written expectation.
objectives: Give every page a distinct title, useful description, canonical URL, and social data consistent with visible content.

Build typed Next.js metadata for an indexable, shareable product page, then prove the result with this exact signal: the built HTML contains a distinct title, useful description, expected canonical, and Open Graph data matching the content.

blocks.text: A high-quality page serves three audiences at once: the person using it, assistive technology interpreting it, and the crawler discovering it. In “Technical SEO and metadata”, the concrete input is a product page reachable through several URLs that needs a title and canonical matching the visible product. canonical URL means: The preferred address declared to search engines when several URLs may show the same content. The model is complete only when you generate metadata from the same validated product source as the rendering, with a stable absolute production URL and can observe that the built HTML contains a distinct title, useful description, expected canonical, and Open Graph data matching the content.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: A web page is a physical shop: its sign must be identifiable, its aisles usable, and its entrance fast enough not to turn visitors away. Here the part you will actually inspect is typed Next.js metadata for an indexable, shareable product page; stop using the analogy if it obscures the technical boundary shown by the code.

Start by bounding this lesson’s case: a product page reachable through several URLs that needs a title and canonical matching the visible product. Give every page a distinct title, useful description, canonical URL, and social data consistent with visible content. The term canonical URL is not a decorative label: The preferred address declared to search engines when several URLs may show the same content. It determines what enters, which authority may act, and which observation counts as evidence rather than an impression.

In exercises/20-web-quality/product-metadata.ts, the example deliberately reduces the system to typed Next.js metadata for an indexable, shareable product page. Read each line as one responsibility, then run npm run build. The main failure to trigger is: all product pages inherit layout metadata and crawlers can no longer distinguish products. It shows why the professional correction is to generate metadata from the same validated product source as the rendering, with a stable absolute production URL, not to conceal the error.

In a real system, the happy path is only one case among retries, invalid input, and partial outages. The expected proof is that the built HTML contains a distinct title, useful description, expected canonical, and Open Graph data matching the content. Apply the same evidence to product pages, search results, and the add-to-cart journey, using a correlation trace without secrets or personal data so both success and failure remain explainable.

items.definition: The preferred address declared to search engines when several URLs may show the same content.
Meaning conveyed by an HTML element independently of its visual appearance.
A measurable weight, latency, or stability limit that a page must not exceed.
